transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, the main thing is my sleep has just… come loose, I guess. It’s not behaving like sleep anymore. At first I’d be up after two or three hours, wide awake, drafting plans and feeling like I could start the day right then—reminded me of when I was in graduate school and thought a legal pad could solve anything, you know. But now it’s different. I’m lying there before dawn, stomach tight, not really rested at all. It’s wearing me down.
Have you ever experienced a period where you felt unusually energetic, needed less sleep, or felt like your thoughts were racing, even if it felt good at the time?

Yes… yes, that’s happened. It’s like I had this engine running inside me, you know? Sitting quietly felt almost impossible. I’d be up before sunrise, already calling people—probably too early, honestly—and rewriting proposals, shifting from one task to the next like if I stopped, something important would fall apart.

It did feel good at first, I suppose. Productive. Though I remember once reorganizing a whole stack of old papers because I’d found a note from a committee meeting years ago—completely irrelevant, but somehow it felt connected at the time. Anyway… yes, I had a lot more energy than usual and I just kept going.
Did this period of high energy and being very active eventually lead to any problems, or did it feel good all the way through without any downside?

No, no… it didn’t stay good. I mean, for a little while I could dress it up as being productive, but then things started slipping. My wife has had to take over the finances—bills, accounts, all of it—and she’s been staying close to me, watching me really, for safety.

And I used to be dependable, you know. The museum, the arts council, friends I’d promised to meet… I just stopped showing up reliably. Which is embarrassing, because I was always the one with the calendar and the proper pen. So yes, there’s been a downside. A real one.
Have you ever had a period where you felt down nearly every day, lost interest in things you usually enjoy, or had trouble functioning because of low mood? Something that lasted for weeks at a time?

Yes… I think so. Or, well, not “think”—I suppose I know. The things that used to pull me right in just don’t. I used to spend whole afternoons at the museum, just wandering from room to room, and I could lose myself in photography or cooking—making something complicated for no real reason except the pleasure of it.

Lately I look at my camera, or even the bridge table, and I just feel… nothing. Not sadness exactly in that moment, more like the weight of how much effort it would take to pretend I cared. It’s strange, because I was always the sort of person who had hobbies stacked up like books on a chair. Now they just sit there.

After that high-energy period you described, did you have a time when your mood dropped significantly, and you felt down, hopeless, or unable to function for most of the day nearly every day for at least two weeks?

Yes… after the big plans fell apart, I went the other way. It wasn’t just a bad week. It’s been, oh, about nine months now, I think.

I sort of withdrew into myself. A lot of guilt, too—going over what I should’ve done differently, which is useless, I know, but there it is. Most days have been low like that. I lose track sometimes because one day starts to look like the next… I used to keep such careful notes, even little lists on index cards, but lately I just don’t. So yes, it’s been much longer than two weeks. About nine months.

Have you had any other periods in your life, besides the one you just described, where you felt unusually energetic, needed less sleep, or your thoughts were racing—something that might have looked like mania to others?

I’m not sure, honestly. My memory for “periods” is a bit slippery when you put it that way.

There were times in life when I was busier, of course—committees, work, the usual mad rush before an exhibition opening. I used to get quite wound up about those, especially if the labels weren’t printed properly or someone hung a photograph crooked. That sort of thing could keep me pacing around, but whether that was what you mean… I don’t know.

Nothing is coming to mind clearly as another stretch like the one we’ve been talking about. But I may be missing something. My wife would probably remember the pattern better than I do.

Can you recall if there was at least one other time in your life, outside of the recent high-energy period we’ve been talking about, when you felt unusually excited, irritable, or full of energy — something that was noticeable to others and lasted for several days or more?

Yes… I suppose there was at least one other time. I hadn’t quite sorted it into the same drawer in my mind, if that makes sense.

I remember feeling almost brilliantly optimistic for weeks, like every obstacle was just… nothing. Trivial. I’d think, “Well, obviously this can be solved,” and I couldn’t understand why everyone else was being so slow about it. There was a kind of shine on everything.

But if anyone questioned me—my wife, colleagues, even someone making a small practical point—I’d snap. Not just disagree, I’d feel as if they were trying to sabotage me, or sabotage the only sensible person in the room. Which sounds awful when I say it out loud. I used to be particular about things, you know, even with museum labels and framing and whether the light hit the glass properly—but this was sharper than that. It went on for weeks, I think.

Can you recall if during any of those high-energy periods, your mood was extremely elevated or irritable to the point where it was clearly different from your usual self, and lasted for at least a week or more?

Yes, yes… it was definitely different from my ordinary self. It wasn’t just being in a good mood.

For weeks I felt almost brilliantly optimistic, like every obstacle was trivial—like anyone sensible should be able to see the solution immediately. And then, if anyone questioned me, I’d snap. My wife would make some perfectly reasonable point, or a colleague would hesitate over something, and I’d feel as if they were trying to sabotage me. As if I were the only sensible man in the room, which… well, that’s not a very flattering way to put it, but it felt true at the time.

It lasted more than a week, yes. Weeks, I think. I remember the feeling more clearly than the calendar.
